facts.fact: Papers that adopted the Model Debate strategy in Table 2: Multilagent Debate (Du et al., 2023), LM vs LM (Cohen et al., 2023), ICL-AIF (Fu et al., 2023), PRD (Li et al., 2023c), MADRA (Wang et al., 2023b), ReConcile (Chen et al., 2023c).
Section 3.4 is titled 'Multi-Agent Debate'.
Du et al. (2023) trialed multi-agent debate in arithmetic reasoning, where agents present solutions and justifications, aggregate responses, and revise answers to reach consensus.
LM vs LM (Cohen et al., 2023) employed the debate approach for factual error detection, where a generating LLM makes a claim and an examining LLM checks for inaccuracies.

The empirical study by Huang et al. (2023) highlighted multi-agent debate as an effective method for automated correction in LLMs, with improvement stemming from model-driven voting among different LLMs.
PRD (Li et al., 2023c) furthered the debate approach by introducing the peer rank algorithm to optimize the consensus process.
The concept of post-hoc self-correction has deep roots in machine translation, often called Automatic Post-Editing (APE).
Section 3.4 discusses multi-agent debate, including examples like Du et al. (2023), Cohen et al. (2023), and PRD (Li et al., 2023c).
